doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Speaking to the audience: Tito Puente, Dizzy and keeping jazz connected
summary: Vega teaches students to talk to audiences, citing Tito Puente and Dizzy, and warns that jazz has become esoteric; recalls 'play pretty for the people' and Cannonball Adderley.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: But this is something that I think — I talk to my students about — because last night it was great because yesterday I had a young man playing bass with me that’s a student at the University. Because my two bass players were out of town, so I called this young man who’s from the state, he’s from Montpelier. And this is — he’s going into his senior year now at UVM and I got him on the gig and I got him on because I figured great time, come on in, figure out what’s going on, I kind of just guided him through what we were going to do. But these cats, what I do with these students is I don’t just talk about what the music is — oh you’ve got to play these chord changes or rather try this scale on this thing. I also talk to them about please turn yourself around and speak to your audience. A lot of young cats are coming up right now and they’ve got this thing going on where they just play this-this-this-this-this. They don’t even talk to the audience. They just play. And I’m like don’t get me wrong, if it works for them fine. I came up playing with people like Tito Puente where Tito would just talk to the audience and they would laugh. I mean I don’t know how many times I’d be in a gig with Dizzy — not playing with Dizzy but in the audience watching Dizzy and Dizzy had that audience in his hand. He talked to them. And it made them feel like they were in his living room. And he joked around with them and then when they played it was serious. So a lot of times I feel that something that’s left out in jazz education is the business part of it. Because I remember when I first got up

here I went to see some of the young cats playing and I told them man the music that you’re playing is the kind of music that you’re going to have seven guys in the audience going, “Hey man wow, ‘Giant Steps’ in seven man, that’s really hip man.” And I would tell them yeah that’s real cool but you know the average person on the street, they’re not going to get it and they’re not going to be there to listen to that. I think jazz in general has always been a people music but it’s getting to the point where we’re turning it into like something so far off and esoteric and cerebral that it no longer connects with people that are not necessarily musicians. You know? So we have to think about the audience and we could still play modern music that swings and is interesting but we don’t — I think we’re teaching the next generation of players to create something that is so self-absorbed that it doesn’t connect to a wide audience. And mind you I mean the folks that come, I posted something on social media recently about — or I talked about it on a radio show — where I was hanging out with some of the folks that support jazz in this community and man, one cat man, this guy’s got like 7,000 CDs in his house and he’s got maybe 8, 900 LPs. And he’s been to every concert. You name an important event in jazz in the last thirty, forty years, he’s probably been to it and he’s not a musician but he knows everybody on the recordings and his room was full of those kind of people. So there are people that are going to be able to sit there and go yeah, man, the real connoisseurs. But what do we do to be able to make the music so that those folks that come into the gig or might be just there and never heard this music, are going to come out going man that was beautiful, that was beautiful. I remember my girlfriend’s mother, when we would go out to a gig she would always grab me and give me a kiss and she’d go, “Okay Raymond, go out there and play pretty for the people.” I’ll never forget that. And I think it’s important to do that. And I am not sacrificing my art. I mean I listen to recordings of Cannonball Adderley talking to the audience. “Hey, how you doing?” And then he would come out and play, you know, something that was really — especially towards the end ‘cause he was really pushing the envelope.
